description: I'm a passionate tech enthusiast and creative problem-solver interested in AI, machine learning, data science, cybersecurity, and innovative technology. I've led a team in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025, earning Global Nominee recognition. I enjoy collaborating, exploring new ideas, and building impactful solutions.
summary:
Earth Jukebox is a free website that turns NASA Earth data into music, so people can hear our planet change. We used the 10 visualizations from NASA's Earth Information Center, including ocean currents, aerosols, air quality, carbon dioxide, lightning seen from the ISS, night lights, forest height and an atmospheric river. Each one becomes sound: a line sweeps across the image and turns brightness, colour and position into pitch, volume and rhythm. There are six sound styles, from melody lines to drums triggered by lightning flashes. A separate player turns NASA's global temperature record from 1880 to today into a melody that rises as the world warms.

This meets the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by giving people a new way into complex data. Blind and low-vision people can hear it, students can learn by listening, and artists and teachers can use it in their own work. Anyone can change the scale, speed and detail, upload their own images in the Studio, and download the music as an audio file and the values as a spreadsheet. Science becomes something you can feel, share and build on.
details:
What it does and how it works : Earth Jukebox is a free website that turns NASA Earth data into music. It uses the 10 visualizations from NASA's Earth Information Center: Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature, Perpetual Ocean 2, GEOS Aerosols, Air Quality Model Runs, DYAMOND Global Carbon Dioxide, A 3D View of an Atmospheric River, Lightning Events Detected from the ISS, Change in Night Lights 2012–2023, GEDI Forest Height and Caldwell 73.

For each image, a line sweeps across from left to right or top to bottom. The image is cut into thin slices, and each slice is measured for brightness, colour, its brightest point and sudden flashes. Those numbers become pitch, volume and rhythm. There are six sound styles: a melody line, brightness, a colour spectrum where warm colours sound high and cool ones low, a flowing drone, three layers (one each for red, green and blue), and percussion, where lightning flashes become drum hits. Users choose the musical scale, the speed, how much detail to use and which way to scan.

A separate player turns NASA's GISTEMP global temperature record from 1880 to today into a melody. Each year is a note, so the melody climbs as the planet warms.

Benefits

  • Blind and low-vision people can hear data that is usually only shown as pictures.
  • Students and the public get a new, memorable way to understand climate and Earth science.
  • Teachers, artists, musicians and researchers can download the music as an audio file (WAV) and the measured values as a spreadsheet (CSV) for their own work.
  • In the Studio, anyone can upload their own image, chart or drawing and turn it into sound.

Intended impact We want Earth data to reach more people. Hearing the temperature record rise, or hearing lightning storms as drum hits, gives people an emotional connection that a chart often can't. Because everything is free, needs no sign-up and works on phones, classrooms, museums and community groups can use it anywhere.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: TypeScript, HTML and CSS.
  • Website: React 19 with TanStack Start, built with Vite and styled with Tailwind CSS.
  • Sound: the browser's Web Audio API. We used oscillators, filters and a compressor for live playback, and an offline audio renderer to export WAV files that sound exactly like what you hear.
  • Image analysis: HTML Canvas reads pixel colours in the browser.
  • Testing: Vitest automated tests check the image-to-sound rules.
  • Data: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio / Earth Information Center visualizations and NASA GISS GISTEMP v4.
  • Development: built with Lovable, an AI-assisted web builder.
  • No special hardware is needed. It runs in any modern web browser.

How it is creative Instead of one fixed sound, every dataset starts with a sound style that suits it: ocean temperature glides like water, aerosols drift as a drone, lightning becomes percussion and forest colours become notes. Users can then reshape the sound themselves. That makes the site a musical instrument as well as a science tool. A moving scan line shows exactly which part of the image is playing, so sight and sound stay linked.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific honesty: the same rules make both the sound and the downloaded data, so what you hear can be checked number by number.
  • Pleasant listening: the default scale is pentatonic, so any dataset sounds musical rather than harsh.
  • Accessibility: clear labels, readable text, simple controls and a layout that works on small screens.
  • Privacy: uploaded images stay on the user's device and are never sent anywhere.
  • Openness: there are links back to every original NASA page and video, with full credit to NASA's data sources.
